title: Elevator System
description: Design an elevator control system — modelling cars, hall and car calls, dispatching requests to cars, the SCAN/LOOK scheduling algorithm, destination dispatch for smart elevators, safety states and monitoring.
author: Editorial Team

blocks.title: What is an Elevator System?
blocks.text: An elevator system controls a bank of elevator cars in a building. People press **hall call** buttons (up/down) on each floor and **car call** buttons inside cars; the controller decides which car serves each call and in what order each car stops. A **smart elevator** uses **destination dispatch**: people enter their destination floor in the lobby, and the system groups passengers going to nearby floors into the same car. It's a popular object-oriented and real-time design question.

items: Passengers should be able to request a car from any floor (up or down) or enter a destination (smart mode).
Passengers inside a car should be able to select destination floors.
The controller should assign each hall call to a car and decide each car's stop order.
Cars should handle door control, overload, emergency stop and out-of-service states.
Building staff should see the status of every car and fault alerts.
Motor control and physical safety circuits (handled by certified hardware).

blocks.question: What are the non-functional requirements for this system?

items: Safety first: software never overrides hardware safety interlocks; failures fail safe.
Low average wait and travel time, with no request starving.
Responsive: button presses acknowledged instantly; dispatch decisions in milliseconds.
Each car keeps working if the group controller fails.

lines: - cars work if group controller fails
blocks.caption: Elevator Requirements

items: **ElevatorCar**: ID, current floor, direction, state (idle, moving, doors open, maintenance), load, stop queue.
**Request**: hall call (floor + direction) or car call (car + floor), or destination request (from floor, to floor).
**GroupController**: assigns hall calls to cars using a dispatch strategy.
**CarController**: runs a single car's state machine and stop order.

blocks.text: Object-oriented sketch: `GroupController` holds `ElevatorCar`s and a `DispatchStrategy` (interface: `assign(request, cars)`); each `ElevatorCar` has a `CarController` with a state machine and a `StopScheduler`.

blocks.code:
(floor panel)  hallCall(floor, direction)            -> assigned car shown (smart mode)
(lobby kiosk)  destinationCall(fromFloor, toFloor)   -> "Go to car C"
(car panel)    carCall(carId, floor)
(car -> group) status(carId, floor, direction, state, load)   (every ~100 ms)
(monitoring)   GET /cars -> statuses, faults

blocks.text: Each car runs its own **CarController**: a state machine (`IDLE → MOVING_UP/DOWN → DOORS_OPENING → DOORS_OPEN → DOORS_CLOSING`) plus a set of target floors. It moves toward targets, stops when reaching one, opens doors, and continues. Safety inputs (door sensors, overload, emergency stop) are handled by hardware interlocks, and the controller simply moves to a safe state.
When a hall call arrives, the **GroupController** asks the `DispatchStrategy` to choose a car, using each car's position, direction, load and existing stops, and adds the floor to that car's targets.

Each car orders its stops with the **LOOK** algorithm (a variant of SCAN, the "elevator algorithm"): keep moving in the current direction, serving every target on the way, until there are no more targets ahead; then reverse. This prevents bouncing back and forth and guarantees every request is served on the next sweep.
Cars report status to the group controller, which forwards it to a **building monitoring** service for dashboards, alerts (door faults, stuck cars) and maintenance scheduling.

approach.text: Assign each hall call to the closest car.

challenges.text: A close car heading the other way may take ages to come back; cars bunch together; some requests wait very long.

blocks.title: Nearest car moving in the right direction

approach.text: Prefer cars already moving toward the floor in the requested direction; otherwise idle cars; otherwise the car that will reverse soonest.

challenges.text: Ignores load and the cost to passengers already in the car.

approach.text: For each candidate car, estimate the **total added cost** of taking the call: the new passenger's waiting time plus the extra delay for passengers already aboard, using travel time, door time per stop and load. Assign to the lowest-cost car, and **re-evaluate** unconfirmed assignments as conditions change. Apply **traffic-pattern modes**: in the morning up-peak, park idle cars at the lobby; at lunch, spread them across floors.

challenges.text: Estimates need a model of travel and door times; display the assigned car only once the choice is stable.

blocks.text: With destination entry, the system knows where each passenger is going before choosing a car, so it can **group** people heading to nearby floors into the same car. Each car makes fewer stops, travel time drops, and the building moves more people per hour at peak. The cost is that passengers must follow the kiosk's assignment ("Go to car C"), and the lobby kiosks become the main interface.
Address failure isolation: if the group controller fails, each car falls back to serving its own car calls and a default hall-call pattern, so people aren't trapped and service continues degraded.

LOOK guarantees each car eventually reaches every target, but a hall call could be repeatedly reassigned. Track each request's **age** and add a growing penalty to the cost function so old requests win; if a request exceeds a maximum wait, force-assign it to the next available car.

quiz.question: What does the LOOK algorithm do?
options: Keeps moving in one direction serving stops until none remain ahead, then reverses
quiz.explanation: It avoids bouncing and guarantees service on the next sweep.

quiz.question: Why can 'nearest car' dispatch perform badly?
options: A nearby car may be heading away and take a long time to return
quiz.explanation: Direction and existing stops matter more than distance alone.

quiz.question: How does destination dispatch improve throughput?
options: It groups passengers going to nearby floors into the same car, reducing stops
quiz.explanation: Fewer stops per trip means more people moved per hour.

quiz.question: What happens if the group controller fails?
options: Cars fall back to serving their own calls in a degraded mode
quiz.explanation: Each car controller can operate independently.
